Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Assume lonely students are in the room: every personal question stays private, and turn-and-talk partners go by seat so nobody is picked last.

Every student in the room

Point to repeat places that are free and fit inside family rules, and treat online friends and faith or language communities as real people of their own.

Slides and notes

Tap any slide to present from there.

Slide 1 · Notes

Open plainly and light. One question to land: “How long does it take to go from ‘we say hi’ to ‘I’d call them at 1am’?” Nobody answers out loud yet.

Slide 2 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Tell a short true one of yours: a first day, a new job, a move. What did it feel like to walk in? Who made it easier, and how?

Slide 3 · Notes

Stand for fact, sit for myth. Notice the split; the next slide shows the answer. Ask: “Who here has a close friend you didn’t like at first?”

Slide 4 · Notes

The answer, once the room has had its say.

Slide 5 · Notes

The next slide shows the answer. Ask: “Why would both people sit there waiting?” Fear of rejection, mostly. Hold that; the liking gap is coming.

Slide 6 · Notes

The answer, once the room has had its say.

Slide 7 · Notes

This one surprises people. Ask: “Where do you keep showing up next to the same people?” Repeat places do the work. The next slide shows the answer.

Slide 8 · Notes

The answer, once the room has had its say.

Slide 9 · Notes

Ask: “What’s the difference between people who know you and people you could call at 1am?” Popular and close are different things. The next slide shows the answer.

Slide 10 · Notes

The answer, once the room has had its say.

Slide 11 · Notes

Ask: “Where do hours pile up fastest in your week?” Bus, lunch, practice, rehearsal, a job, caring for siblings. All count.

Slide 12 · Notes

Let it land. Ask: “If almost everyone is under-connected, what does that make your invitation?” Welcome, mostly.

Slide 13 · Notes

Ask: “Why would both people walk away thinking the other one wasn’t into it?” Each is busy watching their own awkward moment.

Slide 14 · Notes

2 minutes each way, partners by seat. Then ask for thumbs only: “Up if that went better than you expected.” Most go up.

Slide 15 · Notes

Ask: “What’s the difference between ‘we should hang out sometime’ and ‘want to get food after the game Friday?’” Only one happens.

Slide 16 · Notes

Groups talk and report back; the next slide shows the point. If they say “wait for Diego,” ask: “What do we know about the liking gap?”

Slide 17 · Notes

The answer, once the room has had its say.

Slide 18 · Notes

Groups talk and report back; the next slide shows the point. Ask: “Where else in your week do you have ‘assigned’ people you could turn into chosen ones?”

Slide 19 · Notes

The answer, once the room has had its say.

Slide 20 · Notes

Groups talk and report back; the next slide shows the point. If an answer drifts to “just forget them,” ask: “What would Sofia lose?”

Slide 21 · Notes

The answer, once the room has had its say.

Slide 22 · Notes

Private, nobody shares: “Who are your people outside school? Where do the rules at home leave room?” Online friends count; meet in public, tell someone.

Slide 23 · Notes

Turn and talk. Then ask: “Where else in your life does this show up?” Nobody speaks for a group.

Slide 24 · Notes

Let them think of one person and one specific move. Share the take-home link after: hours, the ladder, openers, who to talk to.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain why close friendships take time (the hours estimate and the liking gap), find their next step with one person using the friendship ladder, and leave with one specific move for this week. Nobody should have to say out loud how connected they are.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 3 minEver been the new one? (a quick story)
  2. 7 minMyth or fact, one per slide
  3. 10 minThe hours, the open invitation, the liking gap
  4. 5 minOne layer below small talk (turn and talk)
  5. 3 minFind your rung (private, nobody shares)
  6. 8 minThree moments, one per slide
  7. 4 minYour people live in a lot of places; where else does this show up?
  8. 2 minOne person, one move, this week

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

Myth or fact, the hours, the liking gap, one of the three moments, and the closing slide. Share the take-home link afterward.

Before you teach
Assume lonely students are in the room.

Some 9th graders arrived knowing nobody, and some lost their middle school group over the summer. Never ask for a show of hands about who has friends, who sits alone, or who feels left out. Every personal question in this lesson is private.

Set up the pair-share so nobody gets picked last.

Assign partners (count off, or pair by seat) so nobody has to find one. Give everyone a pass option and an easier question. A student who stays quiet is still taking part.

Being left out on purpose is a different conversation.

If a student describes being excluded, picked on, or targeted, thank them and connect them with a counselor that day. Don't problem-solve it in front of the class.

Know the signs that loneliness needs more than a lesson.

Feeling alone most days for a long time, skipping school or practice because of it, or seeming hopeless or down most of the time. Don't ask about any of this in class. If a student tells you something like this, or writes it on a card, follow up privately and bring in a counselor.

Online friends come up. Respect them.

Online friendships are real, especially for students who don't see themselves at school. Add the safety piece calmly: meet in public, tell someone you trust, bring a friend. An adult who wants a friendship kept secret is a red flag and a counselor conversation.

Keep the hours estimate honest.

The 50, 90 and 200 hour numbers are one researcher's estimates and vary a lot by person. Present them as a rough map. The point is patience, so don't turn it into a quota.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Families set different rules.

Rides, curfews, sleepovers, and who students may spend time with vary from home to home. Name that openly and point to friendships that fit inside the rules: lunch, study groups, a program the family already trusts. "Make a specific plan" can be a plan at school.

The adults at home vary too.

Some students live with one parent, a grandparent, a foster family, or split weeks between two homes, which can cut into weekend time. Say "the adults at home" and let a plan be a lunch table or a study hall.

LGBTQ+ students may find their people elsewhere.

Some students don't see themselves reflected at school and build their closest friendships online or through outside groups. Treat those as real friendships, and keep the safety steps the same for everyone.

Small talk and eye contact come harder for some students.

Autistic students and students with social anxiety may find the pair-share draining. Let them write their answer instead of saying it. Never treat speaking up or eye contact as the sign of a good friend. Social anxiety that keeps a student from things they want to do is worth a counselor's time.

A repeat place doesn't have to cost money.

Teams with fees, rides to practice, and food after the game assume money and time some students don't have. Point to free repeat places: a free club, the library, a volunteer shift, a youth group, a study group. Students who work or care for siblings at home are logging hours too.

Faith and language communities count.

For some students the people who matter most are at a mosque, church, temple, or other faith community; for others there are none. Some students new to the country keep their closest friends online in their first language. All of those count as their people.

What the research says

Adults who had just moved and college first-years took about 50 hours together to become casual friends, about 90 to become friends, and over 200 to become close friends. Estimates vary a lot by person.

Hall, Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 2019

University students randomly assigned seats on the first day were more likely to be friends a year later with the people who sat next to them or in the same row.

Back, Schmukle and Egloff, Psychological Science, 2008

Across five studies, people who had just talked with someone new underestimated how much the other person liked them. Among college roommates, the gap lasted most of the school year.

Boothby et al., Psychological Science, 2018

Strangers asked to talk about meaningful things found it less awkward and more connecting than they expected. People assume others only want small talk.

Kardas, Kumar and Epley, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2022

169 teens followed from 15 to 25: a strong close friendship at 15 predicted more self-worth and less anxiety and depression by the mid-20s. Being popular with the broader group did not, and went with more social anxiety later. One study, a link and not proof of cause.

Narr et al., Child Development, 2019 (University of Virginia)

Young people's time spent in person with friends dropped by nearly 70% over about two decades.

U.S. Surgeon General's Advisory on Loneliness and Isolation, 2023
